ai_summary:
Great Britain's electricity system is currently seeing a total wind output of 10.6 GW, with Scotland generating an estimated 3.5 GW, representing 34.7% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This robust renewable generation brings Scottish carbon intensity down to 0 gCO2/kWh, contrasting with the GB-wide carbon intensity of 53 gCO2/kWh. However, severe cross-border transmission bottlenecks prevent this surplus green power from flowing freely to southern demand centres. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 43.7 GWh via Balancing Mechanism actions, incurring a daily constraint cost of about £2,772,559. 

To replace this stranded clean volume, fossil generators fired up elsewhere on the network have burned an estimated 8,307,389 m3 of gas, releasing an unnecessary 15,303 tonnes of CO2 into the atmosphere. Extrapolated across an entire operational year, the total yearly cost of curtailment reaches an estimated £1,012 million. Recovered through balancing mechanism charges, this ongoing structural inefficiency increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £3 to £4/MWh. These metrics demonstrate the severe financial and decarbonisation penalties imposed by network constraints, highlighting the critical necessity of expanding grid transmission capacity to relieve consumers and fully utilise renewable generation.
